POETRY.

The Crusader’s Return. 
I saw one come on wine dim, 
With a sword, and burnished helm ; 
I stood once with my own old file, 
And watched him, wearily, approach ; 
He took the cup, and drank it off, 
And drank both, slowly, hot and strong ; 
And then he said, with eyes of flame, 
“I have returned, for England’s sake !”

But I, a poor and humble man,
Had seen his deeds in the dusty East.
I knew the price of his renown, 
And how the falsehoods had been sown ;
I knew the widow’s shriek of pain,
And how the children wept in vain ; 
I knew the graves he left behind,
And the shattered hearts and ruined mind. 

He spoke of glory and of God—
Of duty done and triumphs won ;
But brown the blood upon his blade,
And cold the light in his pale sun. 

And I, a poor and humble man,
Just said, “If that be glory, then
I’d rather be a simple knave,
And live and die among these men.”

—A. C. Swinburne.

A traveling man tells a story of a 
neighbor, who, upon the death of his 
wife, buried her in the orchard. A few 
months afterward, he married again. 
One pleasant evening, as he was sitting 
with his new wife in the parlor, she
remarked, “I think I feel a little uneasy 
about this room.” 

“Why, my dear?” he inquired. 

“Don’t you think it’s rather damp?” 

“Damp? Why, no, I don’t,” 

“I think I do. It feels very damp 
under my feet.” 

“Well, I suppose it is a little,” he said, 
“but you know, my dear, I buried my 
first wife under an apple tree, and I 
guess the roots are beginning to interfere 
with the floor.”
